desc:
On a phone keypad the digits 2 to 9 carry letters: 2: abc, 3: def, 4: ghi, 5: jkl, 6: mno, 7: pqrs, 8: tuv, 9: wxyz.

Given a string digits, return every letter string that the digit sequence could spell, taking one letter per digit. To keep the answer numeric, each letter is written as its position in the alphabet (a = 1, b = 2, ..., z = 26), so every word is a row of digits.length integers. Rows may be returned in any order.

Example: digits = "23" gives 9 rows, [1,4] (ad), [1,5] (ae), [1,6] (af), [2,4], [2,5], [2,6], [3,4], [3,5], [3,6].
hints: Each digit is an independent choice among 3 or 4 letters. The answer is every way of making one choice per digit.
Process the digits from left to right with a recursive function that takes the index of the digit to handle and keeps the letters chosen so far in a shared row.

When the index equals digits.length, copy the current row into the result. Otherwise loop over the letters of the current digit: append it, recurse on the next index, then remove it again (backtrack).
editorial: This is the textbook backtracking tree: level i of the tree corresponds to digit i, and each node has as many children as that key has letters. A root-to-leaf path is one word.

Keep one mutable list for the current word. Append a letter, recurse, and pop it on the way back so that the same list can be reused for the next sibling. The number of leaves is the product of the letter counts, at most 4<sup>4</sup> = 256 here, and each leaf costs O(n) to copy, which gives O(n * 4<sup>n</sup>) overall. An iterative version builds the answer digit by digit by extending every existing word with every letter of the next key.
